I'd input the orders so they showed up on the screen in the kitchen, and then I'd delete them. For over a certain amount it needed approval so I only did it once every 5 orders or so. And when my friend would be on shift I wouldn't even have to do that, I'd just tell him to make whatever.
But surely customers would say, "Where's my receipt?" right? How did you pull that off?

I did the same thing and had a few ask for a receipt. I anticipated this so I would only do it to orders that were common. When asked for a receipt, I pretended to be confused and said it must have jammed. Then I would act like I was fixing it. I would pull up transactions history and reprint a receipt with the same order. People never check the timestamp on receipts.

Also, after I had worked there so long, I could tell which type of people would want a receipt and which wouldn't. Most seniors always wanted a receipt but people with kids were usually in a hurry so very few asked. Smooth operation because I was a manager and had a key. I would pretend to hit the screen, announce their total and hit the screen as I turned the key on the register. No one noticed.

To get around TRed reports (logs of items deleted during an order) being noticed, the majority of the ones I did it on were orders that didn't require the grill. Deserts, sodas, coffee, etc. The only thing I did different was that I didn't pocket the money. I would save it and then close an hour early. After counting the amount of money made off of not processing the transaction properly, I would punch in orders during the last hour to make it appear as if the store was still open and doing business.
I would say "oh sorry", and I'd quickly enter their order in and send it through. counting it as a loss for me since I had to ring it up. But 90% of the time people wouldn't ask for a receipt.

I work as an engineer for consumer products. I have a bit of a reverse juicy secret: we don't try to design things to die after X years. Marketing tries to figure out how long you use something, we pick a life based on what around 90% of people need, then we bound our testing by that life and generally won't spend significant resources to make it live longer than that.

Example: you keep your game console 7 years and we architect for that. We discover that 5% of units will have a failure at 8-9 years and it could be fixed for $50,000. We probably won't do anything about it. If, on the other hand, we find out it's robust and will likely live 15 years or more, we'll just pat ourselves on the back and feel good for doing so well. Then document why it went so well so future projects are more reliable.

Edit: if we find too high of a percentage failing just beyond life, we'd probably deem that too risky to having failures within life and would fix it. It's hard to control stuff that exactly. That's why it's ridiculous to think we shoot for a high failure rate at a certain date. Life should be around a 90% reliability point.

I worked until recently in the musical instrument industry- I have a few things which are useful to know if you buy musical instruments and accessories. Thomann, Amazon and Ebay are the best things to happen to consumers in the industry for decades because it exposes the rampant price fixing that is going on. In the company I worked for, with a product which did not have a price fixed by the manufacturer (which is totally illegal in Europe) we would literally put the cost, shipping and taxes into a spreadsheet, and then pick a RRP out of thin air as long as it was a "nice" sounding number, e.g. £499=nice, £476=not nice. Mark up for the distributor is several hundred percent- for the retailer it's between 30 and 50 percent. For a lot of name brands the distributors seriously monitor the price which retailers are selling at, especially online. Most of the big guitar and amp brands do this. I have heard about music shops being threatened by distributors that they will take away another big brand where they are the sole distributor if the music shop refuses to play the game, or they will take away "dealership" terms or similar. Basically blackmail them into price fixing.

Another thing to take note of is endorsements. If you want to play like ~insert musician here~ don't just believe the ads, check out pictures of them actually playing. Even small time musicians are paid thousands in royalties and endorsement fees to put their name to a product. Unless they are the big brands like Fender, Gibson, Pearl etc it's highly unlikely that a mainstream artist actually uses those products. Distributors also have rosters of their "pet" musicians, so you will often find that a musician conveniently endorses 3 or 4 brands all distributed by the same people. Google the distributors of the brand before you believe the hype.
